senses: The basic monetary unit of Kazakhstan; subdivided into tiyin.
A small, typically circular candle encased in a thin metal cup, so that it liquefies completely when lit and burns as a wick immersed in molten wax.
ety: From tea + light, since they are sometimes used to keep a teapot warm. Compare Dutch theelicht (“tealight”), German Teelicht (“tealight”).

senses: One who, or that which, plops.
examples: When Dr. Elizabeth Martin came into my office and plopped down, I knew something was wrong. Liz is not a plopper.

senses: A person who practices nudism.
A former Roman unit of length, equal to 120 Roman feet (about 35.5 m)
A former Roman unit of area, equivalent to a square with sides of 1 actus (about 0.125 ha)
ety: From Latin āctus (“a cattle drive; a cattle path; units of length and area”). Doublet of act.

senses: A type of distilled alcoholic beverage (liquor), often with a herbal or fruit flavoring, typically drunk neat as an apéritif or digestif.
A serving of this beverage.
Non-Oxford British standard spelling of energize.
The German equivalent of art nouveau.
One who batters their spouse: one who commits domestic violence.
One who applies batter.
One who films with a camera.
One who copies media to microfilm.
Lack or absence of morality.
The metaethical belief that nothing is morally right or morally wrong, that morality does not exist.
Involving, or controlled by multiple factors.
Paper produced from the bark of adult Ficus trees.
An art form based on Mexican bark painting from the Otomi culture.
ety: From Spanish (papel) amate (“amate paper”), from Classical Nahuatl āmatl (“paper”).

senses: An insectivorous primate of the family Tarsiidae, having very large eyes and long feet, native mainly to several islands of Southeast Asia.
ety: From French tarsier, from Latin tarsus, from Ancient Greek ταρσός (tarsós, “wickerwork mat"; "broad, flat surface"”).

senses: Watery; damp; soft.
Lacking substance or strength; weak; thin; dilute; feeble.
In disrepair; poorly maintained.
examples: They lived in a tumbledown shack on the edge of the woods.
The cab pulled up in front of a tumbledown cheap ‘villa’ in an unfinished cheap neighbourhood, — the whole place a living monument of the defeat of the speculative builder.

Some distance north of both stations was a rather small and tumbledown shed for Great Central engines, and there was generally one or more goods tank engines outside it, painted black and lined out in red.

senses: A kind of organ stop producing a string-like sound.
The largest kind of bass viol.
A television soap opera presented as a miniseries.
Describing the pelagic zone of the ocean between the photic epipelagic and the aphotic bathypelagic zones, characterized by very minimal light.
examples: For those animals living in the mesopelagic zone, where some light downwells from the surface, a visual predator looking up at them could see a silhouette.

senses: A ball used in the sports of Quidditch and Muggle Quidditch.
child or offspring.
young plant in orchids that develops on the shoot in place of flower after flowering
Wood of any of these trees.
A speaker who delivers a funeral oration (eulogy) for a deceased person.
A person who praises another person or thing.
examples: I consider, that so far as what is called military renown is concerned, the American Navy needs no eulogist but History.
I am his eulogist; but I am not in love with him. If he were to ask me to be his wife to-morrow, I should be distressed, and should refuse him.

senses: A traditional Spanish unit of mass, varying by time, location, and substance but generally around 11.5 kilograms.
A traditional Portuguese unit of mass, usually equivalent to 14.7 kilograms.
A traditional Spanish unit of liquid measure, varying by time, location, and substance but generally around 15 liters.
ety: From Spanish and Portuguese arroba, from Old Spanish arroua and Old Galician-Portuguese arrova, from Andalusian Arabic and Arabic اَلرُّبْع (ar-rubʕ, “one-fourth”) in reference to its making up one fourth of a quintal.

senses: Boneless processed pork or beef rib meat, served at restaurants and fast food places.
A cut of veal or lamb taken from near the rib
An armed incursion of Spanish conquistadors into American territories.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish entrada (“entry”). Doublet of entry.
examples: Each entrada or exploratory venture into regions beyond Aztec and Inca influence went under the assumed sanction of the Christian deity and with the stated purpose of bringing salvation to the ‘heathen’.
It was gold seized from Amerindians, or extracted with slave labour, which helped to fund the entradas organized locally after 1508, rather than gold from Spain.

senses: Not blockable; that cannot be blocked.
examples: The unblockable actions consist of evaluating an expression and performing an assignment.
He had the soft fadeaway jumper that was virtually unblockable and usually on target, and the face-up fifteen-footer, which he used to soften up the inside.

senses: A network of teletypes.
A teletype message sent through such a network.
A teletype device connected to such a network.
ety: From genericization of Telex Printergram and Telex, derived as a blend of tele- (“telegraph, teletype, teleprinter, etc.”) + exchange.

senses: A small, round sweet made of jaggery and sesame seeds.
Any of several sciences that deal with living organisms
A form of red ochre sometimes used to mark sheep.
ety: From rud + -le. Compare German Rötel (“track”), Post-Classical Latin rudellum. Compare to reddle and raddle.

senses: Any of many plants with thorny stems growing in dense clusters, such as many in the Rosa, Rubus, and Smilax genera.
Anything that is sharp or unpleasant to the feelings.
ety: From Middle English brere, from Old English brēr [Old Mercian], brǣr (“briar, bramble”); further origin unknown, perhaps related to Old French bruiere (“heather”) (French bruyère). Compare Old Norse brǫrr (“briar”), whence Icelandic brörr.

senses: The wife of a margrave.
A woman with the rank and responsibilities of a margrave.
Synonym of shuck (“supernatural black dog”).
Someone who, or something that, slings or uses a sling.
A rope, belt, or bag (often with MOLLE design) that allows someone to sling tools, equipment, or supplies.
An American Midwest diner meal consisting of typically two eggs, hash browns, and a ground meat patty, all covered in chili con carne and topped with cheese and onions.
ety: From Middle English slynger; equivalent to sling + -er.

senses: Showing the gums.
To drag or haul, especially with a rope; specifically (nautical) to haul or hoist and tie up by means of a rope.
ety: From Middle English trīcen, trice, trise (“to pull or push; to snatch away; to steal”), from Middle Dutch trīsen (“to hoist”) (modern Dutch trijsen) or Middle Low German trissen (“to trice the spritsail”); further etymology uncertain. The word is cognate with Danish trisse, tridse (“to haul with a pulley”), Low German trissen, tryssen, drisen, drysen (“to wind up, trice”), German trissen, triezen (“to annoy or torment”).

senses: A wood populated with oak trees.
The wood of the oak tree.
ety: From Old English āc wudu; equivalent to oak + wood.
examples: The Marlfox ignored the jibe, listening to the steady ring of axeblades against oakwood.

senses: Holding that a particular mental phenomenon, such as motivation or justification, has an internal rather than external basis
examples: For one thing, many people regard rationality as an epistemically internalist notion, whereas reliability is a paradigmatic example of an epistemically externalist notion.

senses: The quality of being multimodal; employing multiple modes.
ety: From multimodal + -ity. By surface analysis, multi- + modality.
